entities.name: Ottaviano degli Ubaldini
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ottaviano degli Ubaldini, an influential Italian cardinal who died on March 12, 1273, was a pivotal figure in the tumultuous mid-13th century, navigating the complex power struggles between the Papacy, the Holy Roman Empire, and the burgeoning Italian city-states. Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Innocent IV in 1244, Ubaldini, often known simply as "Il Cardinale" by his contemporaries, wielded significant diplomatic and political power during a period defined by the final, bitter clashes between the Guelph (papal) and Ghibelline (imperial) factions. His career saw him serve under five popes, making him a consistent presence in Rome's highest echelons.

Ubaldini's career was marked by a shrewd and often ambiguous approach to the great political contests of his era. While a cardinal, he was a member of the powerful, historically Ghibelline Ubaldini family from Mugello, Tuscany, leading to accusations of imperial sympathies despite his papal office. He played a crucial role in the papal efforts to counter Emperor Frederick II and his Hohenstaufen successors, Manfred and Conradin, particularly concerning the Kingdom of Sicily. His participation in several papal elections, including the lengthy conclave of Viterbo (1268-1271) which ultimately elected Gregory X, underscores his consistent presence and influence in the highest decision-making processes of the Church.

His legacy is complex, reflecting the deep factionalism of his time. Ubaldini's ability to maintain a position of power and influence across multiple pontificates and through shifting alliances demonstrates a profound political acumen, even if it earned him posthumous criticism, notably from Dante Alighieri. Dante, writing decades later in his Inferno, placed Ubaldini among the Epicurean heretics in the sixth circle, implying a skepticism towards the immortality of the soul, a literary indictment that colored his historical reception and highlighted the suspicion his pragmatic approach could engender.

His strategic influence as a cardinal under five popes shaped major diplomatic and ecclesiastical decisions of the era.
